answer.worked:
Interchange $x$ and $y$.

$$\begin{align*}x&=2y^4\\\frac{x}{2}&=y^4\\y&=\pm\sqrt[4]{\frac{x}{2}}\end{align*}$$

Interchange $x$ and $y$, then complete the square.

entries.description:
Syllabus Content
ME1-11-01 solves problems involving inequalities, functions and their inverses, graphical relationships between functions, and parametric equations

Inverse functions
• Describe a function as one-to-one if every element in the range of the function corresponds to exactly one element of the domain
• Establish that the reflection of a point in the line y = x reverses the coordinates of the point
• Define an inverse function f⁻¹ informally as a function that reverses or undoes the effect of the function f
• Recognise that inverse functions exist for one-to-one functions
• Determine the equation for the inverse function f⁻¹(x) of a given one-to-one function y = f(x) by interchanging the variables x and y in y = f(x)
• Compare the graphs of a function and its inverse function using graphing applications, and recognise that the two graphs are reflections of each other in the line y = x
• Establish that the domain of f⁻¹(x) is the range of f(x), and the range of f⁻¹(x) is the domain of f(x), and use this relationship to solve problems
• Graph the inverse function of a given one-to-one function
• Explain that the reflection in the line y = x exchanges horizontal and vertical lines and recognise that the horizontal line test can therefore be applied to the graph of y = f(x) to determine whether its reflection in the line y = x is a function
• Apply restrictions to the domain of a function, if it is not one-to-one, to obtain an inverse function
• Define formally f⁻¹(x) to be the inverse function of f(x) if the relationships f(f⁻¹(x)) = x and f⁻¹(f(x)) = x hold, and use this definition to solve problems
• Solve problems based on the relationship between a function and its inverse function using algebraic and graphical techniques, including determining the points of intersection of a function and its inverse, where they exist

Equation of the Inverse Relation
• The inverse of a function undoes what the original function does.
• The graph of a function and its inverse are reflections across y = x.
• Find a function’s inverse by swapping the x and y variables.
Warning: The inverse of a function is not always a function. That’s why we call it an inverse relation. We will explore this further in a future lesson.

entries.description: Determining if the Inverse Relation is a Function

Equation of the Inverse Relation
• The inverse of a function is not always a function itself.
• Remember: if a relation passes the vertical line test, it is a function.
• Since the inverse swaps x and y coordinates,
  if a function passes the horizontal line test, then its inverse will also be a function.
• Even functions do not have an inverse function, as its symmetry means it will fail the horizontal line test.

entries.description: Inverse Functions

Finding the Inverse Function
The inverse function is the set of original ordered pairs, but with input and output swapped.
\(f=\{(a,A),(b,B),(c,C)\}\)
\(f^{-1}=\{(A,a),(B,b),(C,c)\}\)
If you are given \(f(x)\) and asked to find \(f^{-1}(x)\):
1. Rewrite \(f(x)=\) as \(y=\).
2. Swap the \(x\) and \(y\).
3. Rearrange for \(y\), then write as \(f^{-1}(x)\).

entries.description: Domain Restrictions

Restricting the Domain
When a function’s inverse is not a function, we need to restrict the domain so that the new restricted function has an inverse.
• We call a function invertible if its inverse is also a function.
• A function is invertible when it is one-to-one.
• Make a function invertible by limiting its domain based on turning points.
• Restrict domains so that the curve is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing, i.e., the gradient does not change sign, and include the turning point.
